prompt: In many countries, fewer school leavers are choosing to study science and mathematics at a higher level. Why is this happening? What could be done to encourage more young people into these subjects?
essay:
The retreat from science and mathematics is usually described as a failure of enthusiasm, as though teenagers had simply stopped finding the subjects interesting. The pattern looks different if you follow the incentives. Most of the students who drop physics or further mathematics do so knowing perfectly well that the work is worth doing; they drop it because the system assessing them punishes them for continuing.

Two things push in the same direction. The first is arithmetic: when a university place turns on a small number of grades, a subject with a demanding syllabus and an unforgiving mark scheme is a poor investment, and the strongest candidates are often the ones best placed to see this. The second is what happens in the classroom before that decision is ever made. A syllabus crowded with content that must be recalled leaves no room for the thing that makes science worth doing — the slow, uncertain business of testing an idea and finding out you were wrong — so the subject a student rejects at sixteen is not really the subject at all.

If those are the causes, cosmetic remedies will not touch them. Encouragement campaigns and inspirational talks address a shortage of interest that mostly does not exist. What is needed instead is to change the arithmetic and to restore the missing experience. Admissions can be made to recognise the difficulty of a paper rather than the raw grade, so that a candidate loses nothing by attempting the harder one. Assessment can reward an extended investigation alongside the written examination, which forces curriculum time to be given to laboratory and modelling work rather than borrowed from it.

Neither measure is quick and neither is free. But they have the merit of treating young people as the rational actors they are, which is more than can be said for asking them to be more enthusiastic about a choice that currently costs them.
title: Why fewer school leavers study science and maths
